title: Stock Exchange
problem: Design a stock exchange with a matching engine that processes limit orders, a market-data publisher that broadcasts book updates at 100K ticks/s, and a batched clearing/settlement pipeline.
summary: A low-latency exchange built around a SINGLE-THREADED, in-memory matching engine per symbol. The dominant design choice is determinism over raw throughput: each symbol gets one thread owning one in-memory order book, which makes the match order provably reproducible (critical for audit and dispute resolution) and eliminates lock contention on the hot path. Sharding is by symbol — not thread-per-order — so the exchange scales by adding more symbols to more engines. The market-data publisher fans out book updates via UDP multicast (exchange-native) or Kafka (cloud-native) to thousands of subscribers. Clearing and settlement are intentionally BATCHED (T+1 or T+2) so the hot path stays fast while back-office systems handle the heavyweight legal transfer of ownership.

functional: Accept limit orders (buy/sell, price, quantity, client_order_id) and match them against the resting book in price-time priority
Accept market orders that consume liquidity at the best available prices until filled or exhausted
Support cancel and cancel-replace on resting orders by client_order_id or exchange_order_id
Emit an execution report (fill, partial fill, reject, cancel) per state change to the owning client
Publish market data: top-of-book quotes, full order book snapshots, and incremental book deltas
Halt, resume, and auction open/close per symbol under operator or circuit-breaker control
nonFunctional: Tail latency: p99 order-ack under 100 microseconds intra-rack; market data fanout under 10 microseconds beyond the matcher
Determinism: two replicas fed the same sequenced input must produce byte-identical output
Zero order loss: every accepted order is durably sequenced before it enters the book
Throughput per symbol: 1M+ orders per second sustained on a single matching engine core
Availability via hot-standby replica with sequence-number-driven failover; no split brain
Full audit trail of every order and every state change retained per regulatory rules

assumptions: ~5000 listed symbols, of which ~500 are actively traded
Peak 100K orders/s across all symbols; hot symbols handle 5K–10K orders/s each
Peak 100K market-data ticks/s (every book change fans out)
Thousands of subscribers to market data (brokers, HFT firms, retail data vendors)
7-year regulatory retention (SEC Rule 17a-4, MiFID II) on every order + execution + cancel
estimates: Matching engine budget: in-memory O(log N) per match on a skip-list/priority-queue; p99 <100μs on hot path
Order gateway: 100K orders/s * ~500B per order ≈ 50 MB/s ingress, well within one NIC
Execution log: 100K executions/s peak * ~200B ≈ 20 MB/s sustained → ~1.7 TB/day; Kafka tiered to S3
Market data fanout: 100K ticks/s * 100B * 1000 subscribers ≈ 10 GB/s aggregate egress — needs multicast
Historical / TSDB: bar aggregation (1s, 1m, 1h, 1d) stored long-term; raw tape in cold storage

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client/Broker] --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> gw[Order Gateway] gw --> risk[Order Validation/Risk] risk --> engine[Matching Engine] engine --> exec[Execution Log] engine --> md[Market Data Publisher] exec --> clearing[Clearing/Settlement] exec --> tsdb[(Historical TSDB)]

client.name: Client / Broker
client.summary: Broker or algorithmic trading system that submits orders on behalf of end investors.

sections.heading: Protocol
sections.body: FIX 4.2/4.4 or FIX 5.0 over TCP is the industry standard. Some exchanges also expose a binary ITCH/OUCH protocol for ultra-low-latency firms. WebSocket JSON exists for retail-facing APIs but is not used by professional firms.

sections.heading: Order types
sections.body:
- Limit (price + quantity; rests on the book if it doesn't cross)
- Market (match whatever's there; no price protection)
- IOC (immediate-or-cancel)
- FOK (fill-or-kill — must fill whole quantity or cancel)
- Stop / Stop-Limit (triggered)

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The client-exchange boundary is where most regulatory and audit requirements land: every order has to be attributable to a specific firm, a specific user, and a specific decision. Clean identity at the edge is non-negotiable.

bottlenecks.title: FIX session reconnect storm on gateway failover
bottlenecks.trigger: When a gateway fails, all FIX sessions pinned to it (potentially hundreds of broker sessions at 5K–10K orders/s each on hot symbols) must reconnect within the <1s session outage SLA and replay from the last acked MsgSeqNum.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker EMS shows disconnected sessions; on-reconnect the client floods the exchange with ResendRequests and queued orders, causing a spike well above the 100K orders/s steady-state peak and delayed fills for 5–30s.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement client-side exponential backoff with jitter on reconnect, cap in-flight queued orders during disconnection, and use dual active FIX sessions (primary + backup gateway) with pre-established TCP so failover is a session-switch not a reconnect.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on FIX Logon rate > 10x baseline in any 10s window, ResendRequest volume spikes, or MsgSeqNum gap count per session exceeding a threshold (e.g., >100 messages).

bottlenecks.title: Sequence number desynchronization on client restart
bottlenecks.trigger: Client EMS crashes or restarts without persisting the last sent/received MsgSeqNum (tag 34); on reconnect the exchange sees a gap or mismatch and refuses to accept new orders until the replay completes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker cannot send NewOrderSingle messages for seconds to minutes after restart; orders queue locally; traders see 'session not ready' and miss market moves. Regulator-visible because every order must be accounted for — no silent skipping allowed.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Persist MsgSeqNum to durable storage (fsync'd file or local DB) on every send/recv; use FIX session-level SequenceReset-GapFill (35=4) judiciously; support FIX 4.4 ResetSeqNumFlag=Y only at negotiated session boundaries (typically start-of-day).
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor session-level metrics for SequenceReset messages, Logout with text='MsgSeqNum too low', and time-to-ready after reconnect (alert if >2s).

bottlenecks.title: Client-side order throttle breaches triggering mass rejects
bottlenecks.trigger: An algo bug or market-open burst causes a client to exceed its per-second order quota (enforced at the risk layer); at 5K–10K orders/s on hot symbols a runaway loop can hit limits within milliseconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker receives a flood of ExecReport rejects (35=8, OrdStatus=8) with reason 'rate limit exceeded'; intended fills never happen; in worst case the firm is auto-disabled by exchange risk and must call the trading desk to re-enable.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Client-side token-bucket rate limiter sized below the exchange's per-firm quota (e.g., 80% headroom); circuit breaker on reject-rate > 5% that pauses order submission for manual review; pre-trade notional caps in the EMS mirroring exchange risk rules.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on client reject rate > 1% sustained over 10s, or any burst of >100 rejects in 1s with reason code indicating throttle/credit limits.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Client/Broker is modeled as a first-class component In most system designs, "the client" is just a browser or mobile app and barely worth drawing. For a stock exchange, it's the opposite: the client is a **broker or algorithmic trading system**, and the boundary between it and the exchange is where nearly every regulatory, identity, and protocol requirement lives. The exchange doesn't talk to end investors — it talks to firms who have signed legal agreements, been issued FIX session credentials, and agreed to per-firm risk limits. Every order carries an attributable chain: which firm, which user, which decision. Without modeling this boundary explicitly, you can't reason about session management, sequence numbers, or audit. ## What happens without it If you treat the client as an afterthought and expose, say, a simple REST endpoint, the first real failure is during a gateway crash: thousands of broker sessions reconnect simultaneously, each replaying queued orders from their last acked sequence number. Without FIX's sequence-number protocol baked into the client contract, the exchange either **silently drops orders** (an SEC incident) or **double-executes** them on replay (a financial incident). The order gateway and risk layer get blamed, but the root cause is that the client-exchange protocol wasn't designed to survive disconnects. ## The number that forces the design The capacity plan assumes **5K–10K orders/s on a single hot symbol** from a single firm. At 10K orders/s, a one-second gateway blip means 10,000 orders in-flight that must be reconciled on reconnect — impossible without a sequenced, replayable protocol like FIX. That's why the client runs FIX over persistent TCP with durable `MsgSeqNum` tracking, not stateless HTTP. ## Trade-off FIX is verbose and harder to debug than JSON, but the exchange accepts that cost because every order must be accounted for — no silent skipping allowed.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L4 TCP load balancer (or a FIX-aware session router) fronting the order gateway fleet.

sections.heading: Why L4 not L7
sections.body: FIX sessions are long-lived stateful TCP connections with sequenced messages. L7 parsing is unnecessary overhead and breaks FIX sequence-number semantics. L4 TCP routing preserves the session.

sections.heading: Session affinity
sections.body: Sticky routing per FIX session — once a broker's session lands on a gateway, it stays there for the session's life. Reconnection goes through a session manager that re-binds state from the gateway's session store.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Gateway failure drops the TCP connection; the broker reconnects and the FIX sequence-number replay brings it back to the last acked state. Exchange SLA: <1s of session outage on gateway failover.

gained: Sub-microsecond L4 routing — relevant for HFT-grade exchanges
lost: Dedicated hardware + kernel bypass tuning expertise

bottlenecks.title: Connection table exhaustion from long-lived FIX sessions
bottlenecks.trigger: L4 LB must maintain persistent TCP conntrack entries for every broker FIX session for the entire trading day (6.5h+). With thousands of broker sessions across ~500 active symbols plus redundant primary/backup sessions, conntrack table can approach the configured 50,000 concurrency ceiling during market open when all firms connect simultaneously.
bottlenecks.symptom: New FIX Logon attempts receive TCP RST or silent drops; brokers see 'connection refused' at market open; existing sessions remain healthy but firms unable to establish backup sessions — which defeats the <1s failover SLA when a gateway dies later in the day.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size conntrack table to 4x expected peak sessions (e.g. nf_conntrack_max=200000), tune tcp_established timeout to 24h to match trading day, enable SO_REUSEPORT across LB instances, and pre-warm LB capacity 30min before market open. Consider DPDK LB variant which bypasses kernel conntrack entirely.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on conntrack table utilization >70% (`nf_conntrack_count / nf_conntrack_max`), TCP SYN drop counter increments, or any `nf_conntrack: table full` dmesg entries. Track active session count per LB vs. capacity headroom.

bottlenecks.title: Session affinity loss on LB instance failure
bottlenecks.trigger: If an LB instance dies, all FIX sessions routed through it drop simultaneously. At 5K–10K orders/s per hot symbol, a single LB handling a slice of broker traffic can have thousands of in-flight orders when it fails. Sticky routing state (session→gateway binding) must be reconstructed on the surviving LB or new instance.
bottlenecks.symptom: Mass FIX session disconnects; on reconnect, brokers may land on a different gateway than their session state lives on, causing MsgSeqNum mismatches and ResendRequest storms; 30+ second recovery instead of the <1s SLA; potential for duplicate or dropped orders during reconciliation.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replicate session→gateway routing table to a shared store (Redis/etcd) with sub-second replication; deploy LBs in active-active pairs with VRRP/ECMP so a failure drops at most half of sessions; use consistent hashing on session_id so rerouting is deterministic; health-check gateways independently so LB failover doesn't cascade to gateway reconnects.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB instance heartbeat loss, session reroute rate >100/s, or any divergence between LB session table replicas. Monitor p99 session reconnect-to-ready time with alert threshold of 2s.

bottlenecks.title: Head-of-line blocking on a single TCP session under burst load
bottlenecks.trigger: A single FIX session from a hot broker can push 5K–10K orders/s on a symbol like AAPL. L4 LB does pure byte forwarding on one TCP connection — if the destination gateway slows (GC pause, risk cache miss, disk fsync), TCP backpressure propagates back through the LB to the broker, blocking ALL orders on that session including cancels.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker's send buffer fills; all subsequent orders queue locally in the EMS; cancels for resting orders are stuck behind new orders during a fast market move — exactly when traders most need to cancel. Tail latency on LB→gateway path spikes from <2ms to hundreds of ms.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Support dual FIX sessions per firm (one for new orders, one for cancels/admin) so cancels bypass order-flow HOL blocking; tune TCP send/recv buffers on LB (net.ipv4.tcp_wmem) to absorb short bursts; enforce per-session rate limits at the LB edge rather than letting backpressure build; ensure gateway p99 stays <5ms via capacity headroom.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor TCP send-queue depth per connection on LB, alert on any session with >1MB queued for >100ms; track LB→gateway forward latency p99 with alert at 10ms; correlate with gateway GC pause logs.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Load Balancer sits in front of the Order Gateway For this exchange, the LB isn't doing what it does for a typical web app. It's not spreading HTTP requests across stateless servers. Instead, it's routing **long-lived FIX sessions** — persistent TCP connections that a broker opens at market open and keeps alive all day, pushing sequenced order messages through. With thousands of broker firms connecting, you need a fleet of order gateways (not one giant machine), and something has to decide which gateway each broker's session lands on. That's the LB's job here: **session-aware TCP routing**, not request distribution. ## What breaks without it Without an LB, every broker would need to hardcode a specific gateway's IP. When that gateway crashes or gets redeployed, every session on it dies and the firm can't trade until a human updates config. Worse, when you add gateway capacity for a busy trading day, no existing broker benefits — they're all stuck on the old nodes. The operator sees uneven load (one gateway at 90% CPU, others idle) and the symptom reaches the broker as "my orders are slow at market open." ## The number that matters The design assumes **100K orders/s ingress at peak**, with hot symbols hitting 5K–10K orders/s from single firms. One gateway can't safely absorb all of that — you need maybe 10–20 gateways, and the LB is what makes them look like one endpoint. At ~500B per order * 100K/s = 50 MB/s, the LB is just shuffling bytes at L4; it doesn't parse FIX, which would add latency the hot path can't afford. ## The trade-off By choosing L4 over L7, the designer gave up the ability to inspect or rewrite FIX messages at the LB — but gained the sub-millisecond forwarding latency that a matching engine targeting <100μs p99 demands.

gw.name: Order Gateway
gw.summary: FIX/binary protocol endpoint. Parses incoming orders, assigns a monotonic exchange order_id, and forwards to validation.

sections.heading: Sequence numbers
sections.body: FIX is a sequenced protocol — every message has a MsgSeqNum (tag 34). The gateway validates monotonicity and triggers a ResendRequest on gaps. Critical: the exchange NEVER silently skips a sequence gap — regulators want every order accounted for.

sections.heading: Exchange order_id allocation
sections.body: A pre-allocated range (10K ids at a time) from a central sequencer, encoded to a dense 64-bit id. Fast local handout, collision-free across gateways.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Gateways are stateful for session management but stateless for order flow — an order's path is gateway → risk → engine by symbol, not gateway-affinity. Scale gateways by broker session count, not order QPS.

bottlenecks.title: Single-gateway session fan-in overload at market open
bottlenecks.trigger: At 09:30 ET, thousands of broker FIX sessions re-authenticate and replay queued orders within a few seconds. With 100K orders/s aggregate peak and hot symbols pushing 5K–10K orders/s from a single firm, a gateway hosting even 50 broker sessions can see instantaneous ingress far exceeding its 5000-concurrency sim budget and 1–5ms service time.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 order-ack latency spikes from <500μs to tens of ms; FIX send-queue backpressure propagates to brokers; ResendRequest storms as sequence numbers fall behind; tick-to-trade SLA of <100μs is violated for the first 30–60s of the session.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm gateway fleet 30min before open with 2x steady-state capacity; shard broker sessions across gateways using consistent hashing on firm_id (not random) so a noisy firm can't co-locate with other hot firms; cap per-session in-flight orders via TCP window tuning (SO_SNDBUF) and FIX-level credit; use dedicated gateway pools for tier-1 HFT firms vs. general brokers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on gateway CPU >70% sustained over 10s, per-session ingress queue depth >1000 msgs, or FIX parse latency p99 >2ms. Dashboard gateway concurrency vs. its 5000 ceiling; page at 70% utilization.

bottlenecks.title: Exchange order_id range exhaustion under sustained burst
bottlenecks.trigger: Gateway pre-fetches 10K order_ids at a time from a central sequencer. At 100K orders/s aggregate across ~15 gateways, a single gateway doing ~7K orders/s exhausts its 10K buffer in ~1.4s. If the sequencer call to refill (network RTT ~1ms + allocation) coincides with a burst, the gateway stalls mid-order-flow waiting for ids.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 1–5ms latency hiccups on the hot path every few seconds as buffers refill; if the id sequencer becomes unreachable (partition, GC pause), gateway rejects NewOrderSingle with session-level errors and brokers see intermittent order failures during otherwise-normal market conditions.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Double-buffer the id range — trigger async refill when the buffer hits 50% (5K remaining) instead of 0; increase batch size to 100K ids per fetch to reduce sequencer RTTs by 10x; run id sequencer as a replicated Raft cluster with <1ms p99 allocation; fall back to a second sequencer range on primary timeout.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: id_buffer_size per gateway, alert if <2000 for >500ms. Track sequencer allocation RTT p99 with alert at 5ms. Log every refill event; alert on refill frequency >1/sec indicating undersized batches.

bottlenecks.title: ClOrdID → exchange_order_id map memory growth over trading day
bottlenecks.trigger: Gateway maintains a local map from (firm, ClOrdID) → exchange_order_id for cancel/replace lookups. At 100K orders/s across 15 gateways = ~7K orders/s per gateway * 6.5h trading day = ~160M entries per gateway. At ~100B per entry that's ~16GB of heap just for the lookup map, plus GC pressure from constant insertion.
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway heap grows monotonically through the day; JVM/Go GC pauses climb from sub-ms at 10:00 to 50–200ms by 15:00; cancel latency degrades (map lookup slows as it grows); worst case OOM forces gateway restart mid-session, killing all its FIX sessions.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use off-heap storage (Chronicle Map, mmap'd open-addressing hash) sized to expected daily volume; evict entries for fully-filled/canceled orders after a 5-minute grace window (cancels of terminal orders can be rejected with 'too late'); partition the map by ClOrdID hash to enable incremental compaction; reset the map at start-of-day since ClOrdIDs are scoped to a session day.
bottlenecks.detection: Track gateway RSS and JVM old-gen utilization; alert at 70% of container limit. Monitor GC pause p99 with alert at 10ms. Track ClOrdID map size with daily baseline; alert if growth rate exceeds 2x historical for the hour.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Order Gateway exists in this exchange The matching engine is single-threaded per symbol and processes orders in a deterministic sequence — that's the core correctness guarantee of the exchange. But brokers don't speak "internal order object" — they speak **FIX**, a sequenced, session-based protocol with its own sequence numbers, heartbeats, and replay semantics. Something has to translate between the two worlds: parse FIX messages, validate session sequence numbers (tag 34), assign a dense exchange-internal `order_id`, and hand a clean internal object off to the risk layer. That's the gateway. It's the protocol boundary where the messy, long-lived, stateful outside world gets normalized into the clean stream of orders the matching engine needs. ## What happens without it If you tried to let the matching engine speak FIX directly, every engine thread would spend most of its time parsing verbose ASCII messages and managing TCP sessions instead of matching. Worse, FIX sequence-number gaps (which happen on every reconnect) would stall the engine. The broker would see order latency spike from microseconds to milliseconds, and the operator would see one hot symbol's engine pegged on parsing overhead while the book sits idle. ## The number that forces this split At **100K orders/s ingress × ~500B per FIX message ≈ 50 MB/s** of raw bytes to parse, plus ClOrdID→order_id mapping for millions of orders/day. A gateway fleet (~15 nodes at ~7K orders/s each) absorbs this in parallel, keeping the engine's hot path down to pointer-chasing on already-parsed structs — the difference between a <100μs p99 match and a multi-millisecond one. ## Trade-off An extra network hop (~1–2ms) on every order, accepted in exchange for keeping the matching engine's single thread doing only what matters: matching.

risk.name: Order Validation / Risk
risk.summary: Pre-trade risk checks: symbol tradable, price sanity, firm credit/position limits, short-sale locate.

sections.heading: Pre-trade checks
sections.body:
- Symbol exists and is currently tradable (not halted, not delisted)
- Price within price bands (e.g. ±10% of last close or LULD bands)
- Firm's notional exposure + this order ≤ firm's credit limit
- Short-sale orders have a valid locate (SEC Rule 204)
- Rate / throttle: firm hasn't exceeded its per-second order quota

sections.heading: Latency budget
sections.body: p99 <500μs. These checks are in-memory against state replicated from a config plane (limits, bands) and a position cache. Any network-dependent check is pre-fetched, not queried on the hot path.

sections.heading: Fail-closed
sections.body: Unlike web APIs where fail-open is often preferred, risk ALWAYS fails closed — if we can't verify limits, we reject. A rogue algo order that slips through is an SEC incident.

bottlenecks.title: Position/credit cache staleness across distributed risk instances
bottlenecks.trigger: Risk runs at 100K orders/s across a fleet of instances, each maintaining an in-memory cache of per-firm current_notional and orders_this_second. When a firm's orders fan out across multiple risk nodes (gateway routing isn't firm-pinned), each node's local counter lags the true aggregate. At 5K–10K orders/s from one firm, even 10ms of replication lag means 50–100 orders of uncounted exposure per node.
bottlenecks.symptom: Firm breaches its credit_limit_minor in aggregate while each individual risk node believes it's under limit; post-trade reconciliation flags the overage; in worst case a rogue algo gets 2–3x its approved notional through before any node sees the true total — an SEC-reportable incident.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard risk by firm_id (consistent hash from gateway) so each firm's state lives on ONE risk node — eliminates cross-node reconciliation on the hot path. For firm-level aggregates that must span nodes (e.g. cross-asset exposure), use a Redis/Aerospike counter with INCR + CAS at <200μs p99, or a dedicated risk-state sequencer. Apply a safety margin (95% of stated limit) to absorb residual race windows.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-firm notional_reconciliation_delta > 0.5% between risk-node local view and ground-truth post-trade aggregate computed every 1s; alert on any firm exceeding 100% of credit_limit_minor in the execution log even if no single risk node rejected.

bottlenecks.title: Price band / symbol status cache invalidation lag during halts & LULD moves
bottlenecks.trigger: Symbol status (HALTED, LULD band changes, trading curbs) is pushed to risk-node in-memory caches from a config plane. When SEC or the exchange halts a symbol mid-session, the invalidation must propagate to every risk node within <100ms or orders continue to pass price-band checks against stale reference prices. At 100K orders/s aggregate with hot symbols at 5K–10K/s, even 50ms of staleness = 250–500 orders accepted against a halted or re-banded symbol.
bottlenecks.symptom: Orders accepted during a halt window or outside new LULD bands; exchange must bust those trades post-hoc (regulatory and customer-trust damage); on-call pages from market operations; broker complaints about 'phantom fills' on halted names.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a push-based invalidation channel (Redis pub/sub, NATS, or a dedicated multicast control-plane) with per-node ACK tracking — a halt is only considered 'live' once all risk nodes have confirmed. Fail-closed: if a node hasn't heartbeated against the control plane in >500ms, it rejects ALL orders for that symbol until refreshed. Pre-stage halt commands to risk before propagating to engines.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on control-plane→risk propagation p99 > 50ms; alert on any risk node with symbol_state heartbeat age > 500ms; reconcile accepted orders per symbol against halt timestamps daily and alert on any accept within a halted window.

bottlenecks.title: Per-firm throttle counter reset contention at 1-second boundaries
bottlenecks.trigger: The orders_this_second counter must reset every second for every firm. With thousands of firms and risk nodes processing 100K orders/s, the coordinated reset at each second boundary creates a micro-burst: firms that were at their throttle ceiling (e.g. max_orders_per_second=5000) release queued orders at t=0+ε, causing a saw-tooth load pattern that can momentarily exceed the 5000-concurrency sim budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic latency spikes every second visible in risk p99 (jumps from <500μs to 2–5ms at each second boundary); downstream gateway sees correlated ack latency jitter; HFT firms complain about 'beat frequency' in fill latency that degrades their algos.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace second-boundary resets with a sliding-window token bucket (refill rate = max_orders_per_second tokens/second, continuously) — smooths load and removes the synchronization point. Alternatively, offset each firm's window by hash(firm_id) % 1000 ms to stagger resets. Both eliminate the coordinated burst.
bottlenecks.detection: Plot risk service-time as a histogram bucketed by (t mod 1000ms); alert if any 10ms sub-bucket shows p99 > 3x the overall p99. Alert on throttle_reject_rate showing periodic spikes aligned to whole seconds.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Risk sits between the gateway and the matching engine The matching engine in this exchange is single-threaded per symbol — that's the whole correctness story. It trusts the orders it receives and matches them deterministically. But an order that arrives at the engine has already been admitted into the system, and once it matches, **the trade is legally binding**. You cannot un-match. So somewhere upstream of the engine, something has to answer: is this symbol even tradable right now? Is this price sane (not a fat-finger at $1,862 instead of $186.25)? Is this firm within its credit limit? Do they have a locate for this short sale? That's risk. It's the last checkpoint before an order becomes an irrevocable commitment. ## What happens without it Without pre-trade risk, a single algo bug at a client firm can send 10,000 orders/s of a mispriced BUY into the book. The matching engine — doing its job — fills all of them. The operator sees a hot symbol's book cleared out in milliseconds at absurd prices. The broker faces millions in losses, the exchange has to bust trades (regulatory nightmare), and the market-data publisher has already broadcast the garbage ticks to 1,200 subscribers. Knight Capital lost $440M in 45 minutes this way in 2012. ## The number that forces this design Capacity says **5K–10K orders/s from one firm on a hot symbol**. At 10K/s, a 1-second detection delay = 10,000 bad trades. Risk's p99 budget is <500μs precisely because every microsecond of slippage here is orders that slipped through. ## Trade-off Risk adds ~1–3ms to every order's hot path — accepted because fail-closed pre-trade beats post-trade cleanup every time.

engine.name: Matching Engine (per-symbol shard)
engine.summary: In-memory, SINGLE-THREADED matching engine. One thread owns one symbol's order book. Match logic is price-time priority.

sections.heading: Single-threaded — by design
sections.body: Each symbol's book lives on ONE thread pinned to ONE CPU core. All orders for that symbol funnel through a lock-free SPSC/MPSC ring buffer into that thread, which processes them serially. This is not a throughput compromise — it's a correctness guarantee: the match order is provably deterministic and reproducible from the input stream, which is essential for audit, replay, and dispute resolution. Multi-threading a single book introduces non-determinism that no regulator accepts.

sections.heading: Order book data structure
sections.body:
Two sides: BUY book (max-heap by price, then FIFO by time) and SELL book (min-heap by price, then FIFO). In practice, a price-indexed map of FIFO queues per price level:
```
buy_book[price_level] = FIFO<Order> # one queue per price
sell_book[price_level] = FIFO<Order>
```
Match on incoming: peek opposite side's best price → if cross, pop oldest at that price → fill. Repeat until the incoming order's remainder doesn't cross.

sections.heading: Match logic (price-time priority)
sections.body:
```
on NewLimitOrder(o): while o.qty > 0 and opposite_book.best_price crosses o.price: resting = opposite_book.peek_oldest_at_best fill_qty = min(o.qty, resting.qty) emit Execution(o, resting, fill_qty, resting.price) # price of the resting order o.qty -= fill_qty resting.qty -= fill_qty if resting.qty == 0: opposite_book.pop if o.qty > 0: own_book.insert(o) # remainder rests on the book
```

sections.heading: Sharding by symbol
sections.body: AAPL on engine-1, MSFT on engine-2, TSLA on engine-3. A gateway routes `55=AAPL` orders to engine-1's ring buffer. Adding a symbol = assigning it to an engine. Rebalancing a hot symbol = pause-migrate-resume during a market close window.

sections.heading: Throughput & latency
sections.body: In-memory matching hits p99 tick-to-trade under 100μs on modern hardware. Single-threaded is NOT the throughput ceiling people fear — a dedicated core on a 3.5GHz CPU handles millions of ops/sec because the logic is a handful of pointer chases.

sections.heading: Why not multi-thread per book
sections.body: You'd need locks → contention → unpredictable ordering → non-deterministic matches → audit nightmare. Real exchanges (NASDAQ INET, NYSE Pillar, LSE Millennium, CME Globex) are all single-threaded per book for exactly this reason.

gained: Higher raw throughput on a single book
lost: Lock contention at the top of book (where all the action is)
Impossible to replay exactly for audit

gained: Tick-to-trade in nanoseconds; used by HFT firms and some exchanges

bottlenecks.title: Hot-symbol single-thread saturation
bottlenecks.trigger: A hot symbol (AAPL, TSLA, SPY) sustains 5K–10K orders/s on its single pinned core. With a ~1–2μs per-match budget to hit p99 <100μs tick-to-trade, any order that sweeps multiple price levels (e.g. a market order taking 20 resting fills) consumes 20–40μs on its own. A burst of sweeping orders at market open or on a news spike pushes the engine thread to 100% CPU and the ring buffer backlogs.
bottlenecks.symptom: Ring-buffer depth grows from near-zero to thousands; order-to-ack latency on that symbol jumps from <100μs to single-digit ms or worse; upstream gateway/risk queues back up; market-data ticks for that symbol lag behind competing venues, causing HFT firms to route elsewhere and triggering a self-reinforcing liquidity drain.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap per-order match-loop iterations (e.g. 50 fills) and continue on next cycle to keep per-op latency bounded; reserve the highest-clock-bin cores (3.5–5GHz, isolated via isolcpus, SMT off, IRQ-affined away) for top-10 hot symbols; pre-plan symbol migration to a dedicated engine node during after-hours if steady-state utilization on any core exceeds 40%; use SPSC ring buffers with prefetch hints and struct-of-arrays order layouts to keep the book hot in L1/L2.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-symbol metrics: engine_thread_cpu_pct (alert >60%), ring_buffer_depth (alert p99 >500), match_loop_iterations_per_order (alert p99 >30), tick-to-trade p99 per symbol (alert >200μs sustained 10s).

bottlenecks.title: GC / allocation pauses breaking determinism and latency SLO
bottlenecks.trigger: The engine emits a fresh Execution object and BookDelta on every match — at 10K orders/s on a hot symbol with an average of 2 fills each, that's 20K+ allocations/s per engine. On a JVM or Go runtime, this triggers young-gen collections every few seconds; a single 10ms stop-the-world pause at 10K orders/s backs up 100 orders behind a frozen thread.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic latency cliffs — tick-to-trade p99.9 spikes from 100μs to 10–50ms on a regular cadence matching GC frequency; HFT firms' monitoring shows 'beat frequency' in fills; during the pause the ring buffer fills and upstream risk/gateway experience backpressure; worst case a long GC pause (>100ms) causes a failover trigger.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Object-pool all hot-path types (Order, Execution, BookDelta) with per-thread free lists — zero allocation in steady state; use off-heap flat arrays (Chronicle, Agrona) for the book; if on JVM use ZGC or Shenandoah with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=1 and pre-touch the heap at startup; better yet write the engine in C++/Rust as LMAX, CME, and NASDAQ do; pin the thread, mlock pages, disable THP, set SCHED_FIFO.
bottlenecks.detection: JVM GC pause histogram per engine (alert on any pause >1ms); allocation_rate_bytes_per_sec per engine thread (alert >1MB/s steady-state indicating allocation leak); tick-to-trade p99.99 vs p99 gap (alert if ratio >10x, signaling tail events).

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous Kafka ack on hot path stalls match loop
bottlenecks.trigger: The design specifies the engine waits for Kafka acks=all / RF=3 / min.insync.replicas=2 before releasing an order from in-flight state, adding ~1–2ms per execution. At 10K orders/s on a hot symbol with 2 fills each = 20K Kafka produces/s from one engine thread; if any broker's p99 jumps (common during rebalance, leader election, or ISR shrink), the engine thread blocks and the 100μs tick-to-trade budget is blown by 20x.
bottlenecks.symptom: Engine latency tracks Kafka broker latency 1:1; during a Kafka leader election (10–30s), tick-to-trade p99 balloons from 100μs to tens of ms for every symbol whose partition lived on the failed broker; ring buffers back up; book-delta publication to market data is delayed, making the exchange look 'stuck' externally.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple with an in-memory SPSC ring from engine → dedicated Kafka-producer thread so the match loop never blocks on network; alternatively use Aeron/journaled log (listed as alternative) for microsecond-scale local durability, then async-forward to Kafka; if Kafka must be on hot path, use acks=1 to local-DC replica with an independent cross-DC replicator for the audit guarantee; provision Kafka with p99.9 produce latency <2ms as a hard SLO and alert when the engine's Kafka-wait starts dominating match latency.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric engine_kafka_produce_wait_ns p99 per symbol (alert >2ms); engine_thread_blocked_on_io_pct (alert >5%); correlation alert when Kafka broker p99 produce latency and engine tick-to-trade p99 move together.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Matching Engine is the heart of this exchange For a stock exchange, the matching engine is not "a component" — it's the thing the exchange *is*. Every other piece (gateway, risk, market data, clearing) exists to feed it or to react to what it decides. Its job is to take the stream of orders flowing in for a symbol like AAPL and decide, deterministically and in a provable order, which buy matches which sell, at what price, and for how much. The surprising design choice here is that it's **single-threaded per symbol**: one CPU core owns AAPL's entire order book, and every AAPL order in the world funnels through that one thread. That's not a performance compromise — it's the correctness guarantee. If two threads touched the book concurrently, the match order would depend on lock timing, and you could never replay the day exactly. Regulators require exact replay. ## What breaks without it Without a centralized matcher, you'd have no single source of truth for "what's the current price of AAPL?" Two buyers could both believe they bought the last 100 shares at $186.25. The market-data publisher would broadcast contradictory top-of-book quotes to its 1,200 subscribers, clearing would find unbalanced trades overnight, and the exchange would have to bust trades — a regulatory incident. ## The number that forces this design Hot symbols see **5K–10K orders/s on a single core**, with a p99 budget of <100μs. At 10K orders/s that's 100μs per order average — achievable only because the thread does nothing but pointer-chase an in-memory book, with zero lock contention. ## Trade-off Single-threaded caps one symbol's throughput at one core's speed; the designer accepted that because sharding by symbol scales horizontally anyway.

exec.name: Execution Log / Trade Capture
exec.summary: Append-only Kafka log of every execution and book event. The audit tape.

sections.heading: Topics
sections.body:
```
exchange.order.accepted (every accepted order — post-risk)
exchange.order.rejected (risk failures, with reason code)
exchange.order.canceled
exchange.execution (every trade, post-match)
exchange.book.delta (top-of-book / depth changes for MD publisher)
```

sections.heading: Delivery semantics
sections.body: acks=all, RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2. The engine waits for Kafka ack before releasing the order from in-flight state — this guarantees we never lose a match, at the cost of ~1–2ms added latency. Some exchanges relax this and rely on internal disk replication instead.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 7 days hot on Kafka, tiered to S3/Glacier for 7-year regulatory retention. Downstream: clearing, TSDB, billing, surveillance (spoofing detection), consolidated tape feeds to the SIPs (CTA, UTP in the US).

lost: Less mature downstream ecosystem than Kafka

bottlenecks.title: Synchronous acks=all produce stalls engine hot path during ISR shrink
bottlenecks.trigger: The engine blocks on Kafka ack (acks=all, RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2) before releasing an order from in-flight state. At 100K executions/s aggregate peak and hot symbols emitting 5K–10K executions/s through one engine thread, any broker becoming slow or an ISR shrink (leader election, GC pause, disk stall) pushes produce p99 from the budgeted 1–2ms to tens or hundreds of ms, and the single-threaded engine has no slack.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tick-to-trade p99 on the affected symbol balloons from <100μs to 10–100ms; ring buffers upstream of the engine back up; market data publication lags because the engine thread is parked in kafka.send; on-call sees correlated spikes in engine tick-to-trade and Kafka produce latency dashboards during broker rolling restarts or network blips.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Decouple the engine from Kafka with an in-memory SPSC ring feeding a dedicated producer thread so the match loop never blocks on network I/O; use the Aeron journaled-log alternative for microsecond-scale local durability then async-forward to Kafka; size Kafka cluster to sustain p99.9 produce <2ms with >2x headroom; tune min.insync.replicas=2 with replica.lag.time.max.ms=10s to tolerate brief broker slowness without shrinking ISR.
bottlenecks.detection: Metric engine_kafka_produce_wait_ns p99 per symbol with alert >2ms; Kafka producer in-flight-requests gauge alert >50% of max.in.flight; ISR shrink events alert; correlation alert firing when engine tick-to-trade p99 and Kafka broker produce p99 rise together.

bottlenecks.title: Kafka broker disk / network saturation from 20 MB/s executions + 100K tick/s book-delta fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Executions alone are ~20 MB/s sustained (1.7 TB/day). Add exchange.book.delta at 100K ticks/s × ~44–100B × RF=3 replication, plus exchange.order.accepted/rejected/canceled streams, and a single Kafka cluster sees ~200–400 MB/s write amplified to ~600–1200 MB/s across replicas. During burst periods (market open, news events) peaks can be 3–5x steady state.
bottlenecks.symptom: Broker disk write latency p99 climbs from <5ms to 50+ms; page cache evictions force read-side consumers (clearing, TSDB, surveillance) to hit disk, slowing them further; ISR shrinks cascade; produce latency on the engine path degrades; in worst case, a single hot partition (e.g. AAPL executions) becomes under-replicated and blocks acks=all producers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision NVMe (not SATA SSD) with >2 GB/s sustained write per broker; separate Kafka clusters for hot-path (execution, book.delta) vs. cold-path (order.accepted, order.rejected) topics; partition by symbol with at least 3x the number of hot symbols so no single partition exceeds 50 MB/s; enable tiered storage (Confluent Tiered Storage or Kafka KIP-405) to evict >7-day data to S3 without bloating broker disks; compression=zstd on producers to cut wire and disk volume 3–4x.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-broker disk write p99 alert >20ms; UnderReplicatedPartitions >0 for any hot topic; per-partition bytes-in-per-sec alert >40 MB/s; page cache hit ratio for consumers alert <95%; log flush rate anomaly detection.

bottlenecks.title: Tiered storage / S3 upload backpressure causing 7-day retention window violation
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1.7 TB/day of executions plus multi-TB/day of book.delta, Kafka's 7-day hot tier must offload to S3/Glacier continuously. If the tiered-storage uploader falls behind (S3 throttling, cross-region replication lag, credential rotation failure), hot-tier disk fills toward the 7-day ceiling. A busy day following a backlog event can push usage past 100% and trigger segment deletion before S3 upload completes — a regulatory retention breach under SEC Rule 17a-4 / MiFID II.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka broker disk usage alert at 85%+ and climbing; tiered storage lag metric shows hours of unarchived data; in worst case retention.ms enforcement deletes segments that never made it to S3, creating an audit gap that must be reported to regulators; surveillance and clearing replay jobs fail with OffsetOutOfRange.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size hot tier to 10 days (not 7) to absorb upload lag; run tiered-storage uploader with 2x the steady-state throughput capacity; enable S3 Multi-Region Access Points with failover; implement a hard safety rule: log.retention.bytes cannot evict a segment until tiered_storage_uploaded=true (Confluent supports this via retention.local.ms); mirror the execution topic to a second independent Kafka cluster in a different region as a belt-and-suspenders audit copy.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on tiered_storage_lag_bytes > 500 GB or lag_seconds > 3600; alert on broker log disk usage >75%; daily job that samples S3 for presence of every segment ID in the retention window and pages if any are missing; alert on any segment deletion event where tiered_uploaded=false.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Execution Log sits right after the Matching Engine The matching engine in this exchange lives entirely in memory on a single thread per symbol — that's what makes it fast enough to hit <100μs p99 matches. But "in memory" also means: if that process crashes, every match it just made vanishes. For a stock exchange, that's catastrophic — a trade is a **legally binding transfer of ownership**. You cannot tell a broker "sorry, we lost your $2M fill." The Execution Log is the durable, replicated record that turns an in-memory match into a fact that survives crashes, and it's also the single source of truth that clearing, surveillance, the TSDB, and the market-data recovery path all read from downstream. ## What happens without it Without a durable log, an engine crash mid-session means the operator has to reconstruct the day's trades from broker confirmations and memory dumps — if they can at all. Downstream, clearing has no authoritative tape to net against, so T+1 settlement is blocked. The SEC gets involved (Rule 17a-4 requires 7-year retention of every order and execution). Surveillance can't detect spoofing because there's no replayable history. A single component failure cascades into a regulatory incident. ## The number that forces this design Capacity says **100K executions/s peak × ~200B ≈ 20 MB/s ≈ 1.7 TB/day**, retained 7 years. That's ~4 PB of audit tape — far too much for the engine's RAM, and too hot for a traditional DB. Kafka with `acks=all, RF=3` gives durable fan-in at that rate, then tiers cold data to S3/Glacier for the long-tail retention. ## The trade-off Waiting for Kafka's `acks=all` adds ~1–2ms to every match before the order is considered "released" — accepted because losing a trade is infinitely worse than being 2ms slower.

md.name: Market Data Publisher
md.summary: Fans out top-of-book, depth, and trade ticks to thousands of subscribers via UDP multicast (exchange-native) or Kafka (cloud-native).

sections.heading: Feed types
sections.body:
- Top of Book (Level 1): best bid/ask + last trade
- Depth of Book (Level 2): aggregated quantity per price level
- Order-by-order (Level 3 / TotalView-ITCH): every individual order — used by pros
- Trades: every execution price and size

sections.heading: Why UDP multicast (in co-lo exchanges)
sections.body: 100K ticks/s * 1000 subscribers = 100M fanout events/s. TCP unicast per subscriber would require 1000x the bandwidth and pin thousands of sockets on the publisher. A single multicast group = one publish, many receivers. Recovery/gap-fill happens over a side TCP channel when a subscriber detects a sequence gap.

sections.heading: Why Kafka (in cloud-hosted exchanges / retail data)
sections.body: AWS/Azure/GCP don't support multicast across VPCs. Kafka gives durable, replayable fanout with partitioning by symbol. Higher latency (~5ms vs ~50μs) but dramatically simpler ops for non-HFT consumers.

sections.heading: Sequenced + conflated
sections.body: Every message has a monotonic sequence number. Slow subscribers can opt for a conflated feed (only-latest top-of-book) to avoid falling behind during a burst.

lost: No conflation out of the box

bottlenecks.title: Slow-subscriber induced packet loss and gap-fill storm
bottlenecks.trigger: At 100K ticks/s fanout to ~1200 subscribers, any subscriber whose NIC, kernel buffer, or decoder can't keep pace drops packets (UDP has no flow control). A single burst above steady state (e.g. market open, halt resume, fat-finger cascade) pushes per-symbol tick rates 5-10x higher on hot names, and slow subscribers simultaneously detect gaps and issue TCP gap-fill requests back to the publisher.
bottlenecks.symptom: Publisher's TCP gap-fill service saturates — hundreds of subscribers requesting overlapping ranges from the retransmit buffer; gap-fill p99 climbs from <10ms to seconds; subscribers fall further behind, triggering more gaps (feedback loop); HFT firms complain of 'stale book' and route orders elsewhere; on-call pages on gap_request_rate alert.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Offer a conflated feed (top-of-book-only, latest-wins) for bandwidth-constrained subscribers; serve gap fills from a dedicated retransmit service reading from the exchange.book.delta Kafka topic rather than the live publisher; cap per-subscriber retransmit QPS (e.g. 100 req/s) with 429-equivalent backpressure; publish A/B redundant multicast feeds on separate groups (NASDAQ-style) so one dropped packet on feed A is likely present on feed B.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on gap_fill_request_rate > 500/s sustained 10s; alert on any subscriber requesting the same sequence range >3 times (indicates the subscriber itself is wedged); track per-subscriber last_seq_ack lag and alert when >1000 sequences behind for >5s.

bottlenecks.title: Per-symbol sequence number ordering under multi-engine fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Each symbol's matching engine generates a monotonic per-symbol MD sequence number, but the MD publisher process aggregates deltas from ~500 active symbol engines into shared multicast groups (groups are typically sharded by symbol-range, not per-symbol, to stay under ~256 IGMP group limits on subscriber NICs). At 100K ticks/s with bursts on hot symbols (AAPL/TSLA/SPY doing 5-10K/s each), cross-symbol reordering inside the publisher's aggregation ring can deliver symbol-X seq N+1 before seq N if two engine producers race on the publisher's output thread.
bottlenecks.symptom: Subscribers reject packets as 'out-of-order' and issue gap-fill requests even though no packet was lost; HFT firms observe the exchange's feed as 'less clean' than competitors'; intermittent book-state divergence on subscribers that don't handle reorder; surveillance replay from Kafka shows correct order but multicast shows interleaving.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep the sequence-number assignment on the publisher's single output thread (not on engine threads) so the wire sequence is assigned at the exact moment of sendto; use SPSC rings from each engine to one publisher-per-multicast-group thread; pin publisher threads to isolated cores with SCHED_FIFO; on the subscriber side publish the rule that sequence is per-(feed, symbol) not global.
bottlenecks.detection: Canary subscriber that tails the multicast feed and asserts strict per-symbol sequence monotonicity; alert on any out_of_order_event > 0; correlate with Kafka exchange.book.delta sequence to prove the reorder is publisher-local, not an engine bug.

bottlenecks.title: Fabric-level multicast fanout bandwidth ceiling
bottlenecks.trigger: Capacity plan states 100K ticks/s × ~100B × 1000 subscribers ≈ 10 GB/s aggregate fabric egress. On a real burst day (news event, earnings, circuit breaker release) tick rate spikes 3-5x to 300-500K/s, pushing fabric fanout toward 30-50 GB/s. A single top-of-rack switch servicing a subscriber rack (typical 40-100 Gbps uplink) can saturate when many co-lo subscribers IGMP-join the same hot groups.
bottlenecks.symptom: Switch buffer drops cause correlated packet loss across multiple subscribers on the same rack; subscribers see the exchange as 'flaky during volatility' — the exact moments liquidity matters most; gap-fill requests spike in sync across a rack; post-mortem shows switch output-queue drops, not publisher issue.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard multicast groups across multiple fabric spines so no single switch uplink carries all hot symbols (e.g. split SPY/AAPL/TSLA onto separate groups on separate physical ports); require subscribers to size 25/100GbE NICs with hardware multicast replication; pre-announce capacity (e.g. 'feed guarantees 500K ticks/s peak') so subscribers provision correctly; monitor fabric egress headroom and throttle non-critical message types (e.g. imbalance, auction) under load.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-switch output-discard counter alert at >10/s; correlation alert firing when fabric_egress_bps > 70% of line rate on any uplink AND subscriber gap_fill_rate rises on that rack; synthetic subscriber in each subscriber rack measuring end-to-end loss rate with alert at >0.01%.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Market Data Publisher exists in this exchange The matching engine knows the truth about every price change the instant it happens — but that truth is useless locked inside one thread on one core. Every broker algorithm, every HFT firm's pricing model, every retail charting app needs to *see* the book change, and they need to see it fast enough to act on it. The Market Data Publisher is the component that takes the engine's stream of book deltas and broadcasts them to the outside world. For a stock exchange specifically, this isn't a nice-to-have: if subscribers can't see the current best bid/ask, they'll send orders priced against stale data, and the exchange's order flow dries up as firms route to venues with better feeds. ## What breaks without it If the engine just wrote ticks to Kafka and expected each subscriber to consume directly, you'd pin a separate TCP connection and consumer group per subscriber. The operator would watch the engine's network card saturate, GC pressure spike from managing thousands of connections, and tick-to-trade latency blow past the 100μs budget. Subscribers would see delayed quotes; the exchange would look "slow" externally and lose order flow to competitors. ## The number that forces this design Capacity says **100K ticks/s × ~100B × 1,000 subscribers ≈ 10 GB/s aggregate egress**. Over TCP unicast, the publisher would do 100K × 1,000 = **100 million sends/sec**. Over UDP multicast, it does **100K sends/sec** — the network fabric handles the fanout. That's a 1,000× reduction in publisher work. ## Trade-off UDP multicast is best-effort (packets can drop), so the designer pairs it with a durable Kafka copy for gap-fill — accepting protocol complexity in exchange for fabric-scale fanout.

clearing.name: Clearing / Settlement
clearing.summary: Batched end-of-day job that nets executions by firm and submits to the clearinghouse (DTCC/NSCC in US, LCH in EU). T+1 in US equities as of 2024.

sections.heading: Intentionally batched
sections.body: Legal transfer of share ownership does NOT happen at match time — it happens at settlement, historically T+2 / now T+1 in US equities and T+0 experimentally. The exchange's job at match is to record the obligation; the clearinghouse converts that into a book-entry transfer overnight.

sections.heading: Netting
sections.body: If Broker-X bought 10,000 AAPL and sold 9,500 AAPL across the day, the net obligation is +500 shares. The clearinghouse receives the net, not the gross — drastically reducing the payment/transfer traffic. This is why clearing is batched: netting is only possible at the end of a window.

sections.heading: Integrity checks
sections.body: Before submission: sum(buys) = sum(sells) at trade-level (every execution has two sides); firm-level nets reconcile against the execution log. Any mismatch blocks the file and pages clearing ops.

sections.heading: Output
sections.body: A clearing file (NSCC CNS format in US, SWIFT MT548/MT537 in EU) is sent to the clearinghouse overnight. Settlement happens the next business day; failed settles (e.g. failed deliveries) produce buy-ins and fails-to-deliver reports.

lost: DLT tech is still early in this space

bottlenecks.title: Kafka execution log read throughput ceiling during EOD netting
bottlenecks.trigger: Clearing job must read the full day's executions (~30M rows on a busy US equity day, ~1.7 TB of raw execution data per the capacity plan) from the exchange.execution Kafka topic starting at 16:30 ET. If partitions aren't sized for parallel read or if the consumer group lags, the 120-second expected read phase stretches toward the overnight submission deadline (typically ~02:00 ET for DTCC CNS cutoff).
bottlenecks.symptom: Clearing file submission slips past the DTCC CNS cutoff window; operations team pages at 01:00 ET because `clearing_job.phase == 'reading'` hasn't transitioned; next-day settlement is delayed, triggering regulatory reporting and broker reconciliation incidents.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition exchange.execution by symbol-hash with at least 64 partitions so the clearing worker pool can read in parallel at ~500 MB/s per partition; use Kafka tiered storage with pre-fetch hints; run clearing as a Flink/Spark job with parallelism matched to partition count rather than a single-process consumer; start an incremental netting stream at 20:00 ET that pre-aggregates hot symbols before the batch.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert if `clearing.phase == reading` lasts >10 minutes; track consumer lag per partition with alert at >5M messages; monitor end-to-end clearing job duration against a hard SLA of 2 hours with page at 90% threshold.

bottlenecks.title: Integrity check failure halts the entire CNS submission
bottlenecks.trigger: The design asserts `sum(net_qty) == 0` for every symbol across all firms — any single bug (dropped execution, duplicate Kafka consume, firm_id rewrite during the day) across ~30M executions leaves one symbol unbalanced and the assertion fires. With 5000 symbols and 184K firm-symbol net rows, even a 1-in-a-million data issue blocks the whole file.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call clearing ops paged mid-batch with `AssertionError: unbalanced AAPL: +300`; file generation blocked; no CNS file sent to DTCC until a human reconciles; every hour of delay risks missing the overnight submission window and T+1 settlement.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace the hard assert with a quarantine-and-continue pattern: unbalanced symbols get isolated to a reject file while balanced symbols proceed to CNS submission; run a continuous intraday reconciliation job every 15min against exchange.execution so breaks are detected hours before EOD; use Kafka idempotent consumer + exactly-once semantics (read_committed isolation level) to eliminate duplicate-consume as a cause; store all executions with a surrogate exec_id primary key for dedup.
bottlenecks.detection: Intraday metric `sum_net_qty_per_symbol` emitted every 15min with alert on any non-zero value; daily reconciliation dashboard showing balance trend; alert on any `clearing.quarantined_symbols > 0` so ops has hours not minutes to fix.

bottlenecks.title: In-memory netting map size on very-large-volume days
bottlenecks.trigger: The netting step builds a Python dict keyed by (firm, symbol) holding running totals. With ~184K rows and ~30M executions processed, the job holds the full map plus execution buffer in memory. On a high-volatility day (e.g. Fed announcement, circuit-breaker day) execution count can 3-5x to ~100M+ executions, pushing RSS past single-node limits — especially since the current design appears to be single-process (`nets = defaultdict(...)`).
bottlenecks.symptom: Clearing worker OOM-killed mid-run; job restarts from Kafka offset 0 since no checkpoint; re-read of 100M+ executions takes hours; cascading delay to CNS submission; in worst case the job thrashes swap and hangs without crashing cleanly.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move netting to an external aggregation store (Redis with INCRBY on (firm,symbol) keys, or a Flink keyed-state backend with RocksDB) so memory is bounded regardless of daily volume; checkpoint progress every 1M executions so restarts resume; size the clearing worker with 2-3x the 99th-percentile-day memory budget (e.g. 64GB) and enable heap dumps on OOM for post-mortem.
bottlenecks.detection: Track clearing worker RSS during the job with alert at 70% of container limit; baseline daily execution count and alert if today's count >2x 30-day median by 15:00 ET so capacity can be pre-scaled; monitor GC pause time / Python memory stats during the netting phase.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Clearing sits at the end of the pipeline For a stock exchange, a "match" in the engine is not the same as a "transfer of ownership." When the matching engine fills your BUY 100 AAPL @ $186.25, what actually happened is that the exchange **recorded an obligation**: Broker-X owes Broker-Y some shares, and cash flows the other way. The legal act of moving shares between custodian accounts happens later, through a clearinghouse (DTCC/NSCC in the US). Clearing is the component that takes the day's raw executions and converts them into the netted obligations the clearinghouse actually settles. It's deliberately batched and off the hot path — the matching engine must stay at <100μs p99, and talking to DTCC synchronously on every fill would destroy that budget. ## What breaks without it Without batched clearing, you'd need to settle every trade individually in real time. The operator would watch the matching engine stall waiting on external clearinghouse ACKs; brokers would see fills confirmed but positions uncertain; reconciliation breaks would pile up because there's no netting layer catching sign mismatches before they hit DTCC. ## The number that forces batching The capacity plan says **~30M executions on a busy day**. If Broker-X bought 10,000 AAPL and sold 9,500 AAPL across those executions, the gross traffic to the clearinghouse is 10,000 + 9,500 = 19,500 share movements, but the *net* is just 500. Netting typically reduces settlement volume **10–100×**, turning 30M executions into ~184K firm-symbol net rows — the difference between a feasible overnight batch and a system that melts down daily. ## Trade-off The designer accepted **T+1 settlement risk** (a counterparty could fail overnight) in exchange for keeping the matching hot path untouched by settlement infrastructure.

tsdb.name: Historical / TSDB
tsdb.summary: Time-series store for bar aggregations (1s, 1m, 1h, 1d) and the raw execution tape. Serves charts and analytics.

sections.heading: Why a dedicated TSDB
sections.body: Queries like `AAPL 1-minute bars for 2025-Q4` are time-range scans over billions of rows — exactly what columnar TSDBs (ClickHouse, InfluxDB, kdb+) are tuned for. Shoving this into the matching engine's Kafka log would make every `1-minute OHLC` query an O(N) scan of raw trades.

sections.heading: Aggregation pipeline
sections.body: A Flink / materialize job consumes exchange.execution and writes 1s bars in real-time; 1m/1h/1d bars are roll-ups from the 1s table. Raw tape (every execution) kept in cold tier for 7+ years (SEC retention).

sections.heading: Read QPS
sections.body: Charts APIs serve 10K+ QPS at market open. Pre-aggregated bars + Redis read-through cache → p99 <50ms for a 5-year daily chart.

gained: Open source; widely adopted in finance
lost: Eventual consistency on ingest; not transactional

gained: Industry-standard for tick databases; unbeatable per-core perf

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification from 100K ticks/s ingest into columnar storage
bottlenecks.trigger: The Flink aggregation job consumes exchange.execution (100K executions/s peak, ~20 MB/s) and exchange.book.delta (100K ticks/s) and writes 1s bars for ~500 active symbols every second = 500 inserts/s baseline, but raw tape retention requires persisting every execution (~1.7 TB/day). ClickHouse/InfluxDB merge-on-write amplifies this 3-5x during background part merges.
bottlenecks.symptom: TSDB ingest lag grows from seconds to minutes during market hours; 1s-bar queries return stale data (missing the most recent minute); disk I/O saturates during merges causing query p99 to spike from 50ms to multi-second; on-call sees MergeTree parts count climbing past 300 per partition.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use ClickHouse with ReplicatedMergeTree partitioned by (toYYYYMMDD(ts), symbol_bucket); batch inserts at 1-second granularity (not per-row) with 10K+ rows per block; separate hot tier (NVMe, last 7 days) from cold tier (S3-backed MergeTree, 7-year retention); pre-aggregate 1s→1m→1h→1d in Flink before write so TSDB only stores bars, not raw executions (raw tape goes to S3/Glacier directly from Kafka tiered storage).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ClickHouse `system.parts` count > 300 per partition; ingest lag metric (now - max(bucket_start)) > 5s; disk write IOPS > 80% of device capacity; Flink consumer lag on exchange.execution > 10s.

bottlenecks.title: Read QPS spike at market open overwhelms query layer
bottlenecks.trigger: Design states 10K+ QPS at market open for chart APIs. With 2000 concurrency budget in the sim, a burst above 10K/s (e.g., 9:30 ET when every retail app simultaneously loads AAPL/TSLA/SPY 1-day charts) saturates the TSDB. A single 5-year daily chart query scans ~1250 rows per symbol — manageable — but 10K concurrent such queries hit the same hot symbols and the same recent partitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Chart API p99 blows past the 50ms SLA to multi-second; retail users see spinners/blank charts at market open (the worst possible UX moment); TSDB CPU pegged at 100%; Redis cache miss rate spikes because the cache is cold for intraday bars just-written.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Aggressive Redis read-through cache with tiered TTL (1d bars cached 1h, 1m bars cached 10s, 1s bars cached 1s); pre-warm cache for top-100 symbols 15min before open; separate read replicas for chart/analytics workload vs. surveillance/clearing; use ClickHouse Distributed tables with shard-by-symbol so hot symbols don't co-locate; rate-limit unauthenticated chart API at 100 QPS per IP.
bottlenecks.detection: Track chart API p99 latency with alert at 100ms; Redis hit ratio alert if <90%; TSDB query queue depth alert at >500; per-symbol QPS dashboard to identify hot-symbol concentration.

bottlenecks.title: Cold-tier retrieval latency for 7-year regulatory queries
bottlenecks.trigger: SEC Rule 17a-4 requires 7-year retention of raw tape (~1.7 TB/day × 252 trading days × 7 years ≈ 3 PB). Surveillance/legal queries (e.g., 'replay every AAPL execution on 2021-03-15 for a spoofing investigation') hit cold-tier S3/Glacier storage where retrieval is measured in minutes-to-hours for Glacier Deep Archive, not milliseconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Compliance team submits a subpoena response query and waits 4-12 hours for data to materialize; surveillance replay jobs for spoofing detection run overnight instead of on-demand; in worst case a regulator deadline (e.g., 72h response window) is missed because the retrieval request was queued behind other Glacier restores.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier storage by access pattern: last 90 days on ClickHouse hot tier (NVMe), 90d-2y on S3 Standard with ClickHouse S3-backed MergeTree (queryable with ~100ms penalty), 2y-7y on S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (ms latency, higher cost than Deep Archive but queryable); maintain a separate parquet-on-S3 archive of executions partitioned by (date, symbol) so targeted restores pull KBs not TBs; pre-stage regulatory-common queries as materialized summaries.
bottlenecks.detection: Track cold-tier query latency with alert if p99 > 1min for Instant Retrieval tier; monitor S3 restore request queue depth; quarterly fire-drill querying random historical dates to validate retrieval SLA; alert on any compliance query exceeding 1h end-to-end.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Historical / TSDB exists in this exchange The matching engine and Kafka execution log together give you a perfect record of *what happened* — every order, every fill, in sequence. But that record is shaped for durability and replay, not for answering questions like "show me AAPL's 1-minute bars for the last 6 months" or "render a 5-year daily chart." Those are the queries that power every broker's charting UI, every retail trading app, every quant's backtest. The TSDB exists because the exchange has to serve those queries at scale, and the raw Kafka tape is the wrong shape for them. ## What happens without it If charting APIs hit the Kafka execution log directly, every "show me today's 1-minute AAPL bars" request becomes a full scan over millions of raw executions, aggregating on the fly. At market open, when 10K+ QPS of chart requests hit simultaneously, the Kafka brokers get hammered by scan traffic that was supposed to be reserved for clearing and surveillance. Retail users see spinners; the broker's app looks broken; Kafka's consumer lag spikes and clearing's end-of-day job falls behind too. ## The number that forces this design The capacity plan says **10K+ QPS at market open** for chart queries. A 5-year daily chart is ~1,250 rows per symbol — trivial from a pre-aggregated `bars_1d` table (p99 <50ms with a Redis read-through), but a disaster if computed live from the 1.7 TB/day raw tape. Pre-aggregating 1s → 1m → 1h → 1d bars in Flink turns an O(N) scan over billions of rows into an O(1) lookup. ## Trade-off The designer accepted eventual consistency on bar data (ingest lag of seconds) in exchange for fast, cheap historical reads — acceptable because charts aren't the source of truth; the execution log is.

operations.title: Place limit order (matches against book)
operations.name: Place limit order (matches against book)
operations.description: Broker submits a BUY limit order for AAPL at 186.25. The book has resting sells at 186.25 and lower — the order crosses, matches partially, and the remainder rests on the book.

steps.title: Broker sends NewOrderSingle via FIX
steps.action: Broker's execution management system sends a FIX 35=D NewOrderSingle over its persistent TCP session to the exchange.

steps.title: L4 LB routes to the gateway hosting this session
steps.action: Pure TCP forwarding on an established connection. FIX session is sticky to BROKER_X's assigned gateway — the LB doesn't parse messages, it just moves bytes.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# L4 pass-through — no FIX parsing at the LB
forward(tcp_conn → gateway_assigned_to(session_id))

steps.title: Gateway parses FIX, validates sequence, assigns exchange order_id
steps.action: Gateway reads tag 34 (MsgSeqNum) and confirms it's the expected next number. Parses the NewOrderSingle. Allocates a dense exchange-side order_id (eg 10_400_521_903) from its pre-fetched range. Echoes back an ExecReport 35=8 with ExecType=0 (New).
steps.codeOrCommand:
msg = fix.parse(bytes)
assert msg.tag(34) == self.sessions[msg.sender].expected_seq # 4215 == 4215
self.sessions[msg.sender].expected_seq = 4216 order_id = self.id_buffer.pop # 10_400_521_903, collision-free # ExecReport New (35=8, 150=0) — acks the order back to the broker
fix.send(msg.sender, ExecReport( ClOrdID="CLORDID_9921", OrderID=order_id, ExecType="0", OrdStatus="0", LeavesQty=100)) # Route to risk by symbol
risk_check(InternalOrder( order_id=order_id, firm="BROKER_X", symbol="AAPL", side="B", qty=100, price_minor=1862500, order_type="LIMIT", tif="DAY"))
steps.note: price_minor = 1862500 stores $186.25 as an integer (cents * 100, i.e. $1.8625 tick precision for US equities). Prices follow the same no-floats rule as money.

steps.title: Pre-trade risk checks — all in-memory, <500μs budget
steps.action: Checks symbol status, price bands (LULD), firm credit, short-sale locate (n/a for BUY), and per-firm throttle. All in-memory against cached state.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# symbol tradable?
assert symbol_state["AAPL"].status == "OPEN" # not halted # price band (LULD ±5%)
ref = symbol_state["AAPL"].ref_price_minor # 1860000 = $186.00
assert abs(order.price_minor - ref) <= ref * 0.05 # firm credit — order notional + firm's current exposure
notional = order.qty * order.price_minor # 100 * 1862500 = 186,250,000 minor = $18,625
firm = firm_state["BROKER_X"]
assert firm.current_notional + notional <= firm.credit_limit_minor # throttle
assert firm.orders_this_second < firm.max_orders_per_second # all checks passed — forward to engine
engine_ring_buffer["AAPL"].push(order)

steps.title: AAPL matching engine processes the order (single-threaded, in-memory)
steps.action: The AAPL engine's dedicated thread dequeues the order from its ring buffer and processes it serially against the in-memory book. This BUY @186.25 crosses the resting SELL book where the best ask is 186.24. Price-time priority matches against the oldest resting 60 @186.24, then the next 40 @186.25, filling 100 exactly.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Single-threaded, no locks. This entire block runs on ONE pinned core.
o = ring.pop # 10400521903, BUY 100 @ 186.25 remaining = o.qty
fills = # while opposite side's best crosses our price
while remaining > 0 and sell_book.best_price_minor <= o.price_minor: resting = sell_book.peek_oldest_at_best fill_qty = min(remaining, resting.qty) # Execution fills at the RESTING order's price (price improvement accrues to taker) fills.append(Execution( buyer_order_id = o.order_id, seller_order_id= resting.order_id, qty = fill_qty, price_minor = resting.price_minor, ts = now_ns )) remaining -= fill_qty resting.qty -= fill_qty if resting.qty == 0: sell_book.pop_oldest_at_best # Remainder (if any) rests on our side
if remaining > 0: buy_book.insert(Order(..., qty=remaining)) # Emit events to the execution log and market-data publisher (parallel)
for f in fills: kafka.emit("exchange.execution", f) # audit + clearing
md.publish("book.delta", top_of_book_snapshot) # market data

stateAfter.book_aapl.sell[186.25]: FIFO[ord_9812_qty_110, ord_9813_qty_75] (60→ord_9812 partially consumed? no — 40 matched at.25 came from ord_9812 head)

steps.decision: order crossed — matched 100 shares in 2 fills; no remainder
steps.note: Single-threaded means this entire while-loop is atomic from any other order's perspective. No other thread is touching this book. That deterministic serialization is the correctness guarantee.

steps.title: Execution log appends 2 executions (durable, replicated)
steps.action: The engine publishes each fill to the execution Kafka topic with acks=all, RF=3. The engine waits for the ack before releasing the order from in-flight state — this is what guarantees no fill is ever lost on engine crash.

steps.title: Market Data Publisher broadcasts the book delta (fire-and-forget)
steps.action: In parallel with the execution log write, the engine pushes a book delta to the market data publisher. This fans out via UDP multicast to every subscriber — brokers, HFT firms, retail data vendors — in a single send.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# UDP multicast on the MD group
md_packet = ITCH_SystemEvent.encode({ "msg_type": "R", # R = Stock Related State (top of book update) "symbol": "AAPL", "best_bid_px": 1862000, "best_bid_sz": 200, "best_ask_px": 1862500, "best_ask_sz": 110, "last_trade_px":1862500, "last_trade_sz":40, "seq": md_seq + 1, "ts_ns": now_ns
})
udp_multicast.send(group="239.255.1.20:30501", data=md_packet)
steps.note: One send → 1200 subscribers receive it. TCP unicast would need 1200 sends. This is why exchange-native feeds are multicast.

steps.title: Gateway sends ExecReport(Filled) back to broker
steps.action: Gateway constructs FIX 35=8 ExecReport messages — one per fill plus a final aggregate. LeavesQty=0, CumQty=100.

steps.title: LB passes ExecReport bytes back to broker
Broker receives Filled confirmations
steps.action: Broker's EMS shows the order as Filled, 100 @ 186.246 average. Tick-to-trade latency (order in → ack back) is typically 100–500μs in co-location; 5–20ms over public internet.

operations.title: Cancel order
operations.name: Cancel order
operations.description: Broker sends OrderCancelRequest for an order resting on the book. Engine locates it by exchange order_id, removes it, emits a CancelAck.

steps.title: Broker sends OrderCancelRequest (35=F)
steps.codeOrCommand:
8=FIX.4.4|9=...|35=F|49=BROKER_X|56=EXCHANGE|34=4220|
11=CANCEL_CLORDID_9922|41=CLORDID_9900|55=AAPL|54=1|60=...|10=...|
# tag 41 = OrigClOrdID referencing the resting order

steps.title: L4 LB passes to session's gateway
Gateway maps ClOrdID→exchange order_id, forwards cancel
steps.action: Gateway looks up the resting exchange order_id from its local ClOrdID map, validates the session owns the order, and enqueues a CANCEL on the AAPL engine's ring buffer.
steps.codeOrCommand:
msg = fix.parse(bytes)
exchange_order_id = self.clordid_map[(msg.sender, msg.OrigClOrdID)]
assert order_owner[exchange_order_id] == msg.sender # firms can only cancel their own engine_ring_buffer["AAPL"].push( CancelRequest(exchange_order_id=exchange_order_id, cancel_clordid=msg.ClOrdID, firm=msg.sender)
)

steps.title: Cancel skips pre-trade risk — just a fast ownership check
steps.action: Cancels don't increase exposure, so risk does only an ownership sanity check in the gateway; the engine is next.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Minimal check — cancels never increase credit exposure
# (ownership already enforced in gateway)
pass

steps.title: AAPL engine removes the order from the book
steps.action: Single-threaded engine dequeues the cancel, looks up the order by exchange order_id in the book index, and removes it from its price-level FIFO. If the order isn't found (already filled or already canceled), emits CancelReject.
steps.codeOrCommand:
c = ring.pop
order = book.index.get(c.exchange_order_id)
if order is None or order.state!= "RESTING": # already filled/canceled — tell broker emit CancelReject(reason="TOO_LATE") return # Remove from price-level FIFO; fix up linked list
book.price_level(order.side, order.price_minor).remove(order)
book.index.pop(c.exchange_order_id)
order.state = "CANCELED" kafka.emit("exchange.order.canceled", {"order_id": c.exchange_order_id, "ts_ns": now_ns})
md.publish("book.delta", top_of_book_snapshot) # top of book may change
steps.decision: order found and resting — canceled successfully

steps.title: Execution log records the cancellation (durable)
steps.codeOrCommand:
kafka.produce( topic="exchange.order.canceled", key="AAPL", value={ "order_id": 10400518822, "cancel_clordid": "CANCEL_CLORDID_9922", "firm": "BROKER_X", "ts_ns": now_ns }, acks="all"
)

steps.title: Market data publisher broadcasts updated book
steps.action: Cancellation changes the book — publish the new top-of-book snapshot (or delta). All subscribers see the update within microseconds.
steps.codeOrCommand:
udp_multicast.send(group="239.255.1.20:30501", data=ITCH_OrderDelete.encode({ "order_id": 10400518822, "symbol": "AAPL", "seq": md_seq + 1
}))

steps.title: Gateway sends CancelAck (ExecReport 35=8, 150=4) to broker
steps.codeOrCommand:
fix.send("BROKER_X", ExecReport( ClOrdID="CANCEL_CLORDID_9922", OrigClOrdID="CLORDID_9900", OrderID=10400518822, ExecType="4", OrdStatus="4" # 4 = Canceled
))

steps.title: LB returns bytes to broker
Broker sees order canceled
steps.action: Broker's EMS marks the order as Canceled. Total cancel latency in co-lo: 50–200μs.

operations.title: Market data tick publication (100K/s fanout)
operations.name: Market data tick publication (100K/s fanout)
operations.description: Every accepted, canceled, or filled order mutates the book. The publisher fans out the resulting tick to ~1200 subscribers via UDP multicast. This is the hottest path in the entire design.
