steps.title: Engine produces book delta after a book-changing event
steps.action: Any order-book mutation (new resting order, cancel, fill) generates a book delta with a monotonic sequence number. The engine writes it to an in-memory ring buffer consumed by the MD publisher.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# In the same single-threaded engine loop, after processing an order:
delta = BookDelta( symbol = "AAPL", event_type = "ADD_ORDER", # or MODIFY / DELETE / TRADE side = "B", price_minor = 1862000, qty = 200, order_id = 10400521950, ts_ns = now_ns, seq = self.next_seq # per-symbol monotonic
)
self.md_ring.push(delta) # lock-free SPSC ring to the MD publisher

steps.title: MD publisher encodes the tick into the wire format
steps.action: Publisher pops from the ring, encodes into NASDAQ TotalView-ITCH or the exchange's binary format. Sequence number is preserved — subscribers use it to detect gaps.
steps.codeOrCommand:
delta = self.ring.pop # ITCH-style fixed-width binary — compact, fast to parse
packet = bytearray(44)
pack_into(">", packet, 0, b'A', # msg_type 'A' = Add Order delta.seq.to_bytes(8, 'big'), delta.ts_ns.to_bytes(8, 'big'), delta.order_id.to_bytes(8, 'big'), b'B' if delta.side == 'B' else b'S', delta.qty.to_bytes(4, 'big'), delta.symbol.encode.ljust(8, b' '), delta.price_minor.to_bytes(4, 'big')
)

steps.title: Publisher sends ONE UDP packet to the multicast group
steps.action: A single sendto on a multicast socket. The network fabric replicates to every subscriber that has IGMP-joined the group. ~1200 subscribers receive the same packet; the publisher does ONE send.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# One kernel call, thousand-way fanout
udp_multicast_sock.sendto( packet, ("239.255.1.20", 30501) # MD group for AAPL book deltas
) # Parallel: also produce a durable copy to Kafka for replay/recovery
kafka.produce(topic="exchange.book.delta", key="AAPL", value=packet, acks="all")
steps.note: 100K ticks/s * 44B = 4.4 MB/s out of the publisher — trivial. 1217 subscribers getting 4.4 MB/s = ~5.4 GB/s through the fabric — that's what multicast is for.

steps.title: Kafka writes a durable copy for replay / gap fill
steps.action: UDP multicast is best-effort — it can drop packets. A durable Kafka copy gives slow/restarted subscribers a reliable way to catch up. Subscribers detect a sequence gap and pull the missing range from Kafka.

steps.title: TSDB pipeline consumes the delta for bar aggregation (async)
steps.action: A separate Flink/materialize job tails exchange.book.delta (and exchange.execution) and writes 1-second OHLCV bars into the TSDB. This does not run on the hot path — it's downstream of Kafka with seconds-level lag.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Flink job, windowed 1s tumbling
flink_job.consume("exchange.execution").key_by("symbol").window(TumblingEventTime(seconds=1)).aggregate(OHLCV).sink(tsdb.insert_bar) # Example materialized row written:
INSERT INTO bars_1s (symbol, bucket_start, open, high, low, close, volume)
VALUES ('AAPL', '2026-04-24T14:12:03Z', 186.24, 186.25, 186.24, 186.25, 100);

steps.title: Subscribers receive the tick and update their local book
steps.action: Each subscriber's MD handler sees the packet, checks sequence monotonicity, and updates its local book replica. If a gap is detected, it triggers a gap-fill over TCP or from Kafka. End-to-end publisher → subscriber latency in co-lo: 10–50μs. Over the public internet (retail data): 20–200ms depending on geo and hops.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# subscriber side (broker / HFT firm / data vendor)
pkt = recv_udp(mc_sock)
if pkt.seq == self.last_seq + 1: self.local_book.apply(pkt) self.last_seq = pkt.seq
else: # sequence gap — request replay self.request_gap_fill(self.last_seq + 1, pkt.seq - 1)
steps.note: Subscribers range from microsecond-sensitive HFT firms to retail chart websites. The same multicast feed serves all of them; latency difference is downstream network, not exchange.

operations.title: Clearing & settlement batch (end of day)
operations.name: Clearing & settlement batch (end of day)
operations.description: After market close, the clearing job tails the day's executions, nets them by firm, and submits to the clearinghouse for T+1 settlement.

steps.title: Job starts at 16:30 ET (market close + 30min) — begins reading the day's executions
steps.action: Scheduled job kicks off post-close. First step is to read every execution for the trading day from the Kafka log.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# consume exchange.execution for today's partitions
consumer = kafka.consumer(topics=["exchange.execution"], group="clearing-2026-04-24")
consumer.seek_to_timestamp(today_open_utc)
executions = for msg in consumer: if msg.timestamp >= today_close_utc: break executions.append(msg.value)

steps.title: Kafka streams the day's executions (~billions of rows on busy days)
steps.action: High-throughput sequential read from Kafka. Partitioned by symbol, consumed in parallel by the clearing job's worker pool.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Consumer pulls partitioned records; typical daily count on a busy US equity day
# ~30M executions total across ~5000 symbols
# Read throughput: ~500 MB/s sustained per partition

steps.title: Net positions by (firm, symbol)
steps.action: Build a per-firm per-symbol net. Buys and sells offset within the same firm — only the net obligation goes to the clearinghouse. This is the whole point of batched clearing.
steps.codeOrCommand:
nets = defaultdict(lambda: {"net_qty": 0, "net_notional_minor": 0}) for ex in executions: # buy side buy_key = (ex.buy_firm, ex.symbol) nets[buy_key]["net_qty"] += ex.qty nets[buy_key]["net_notional_minor"] += ex.qty * ex.price_minor # sell side (negative qty) sell_key = (ex.sell_firm, ex.symbol) nets[sell_key]["net_qty"] -= ex.qty nets[sell_key]["net_notional_minor"] -= ex.qty * ex.price_minor # Integrity check: sum of nets for each symbol MUST be zero
by_symbol = defaultdict(int)
for (firm, sym), pos in nets.items: by_symbol[sym] += pos["net_qty"]
for sym, total in by_symbol.items: assert total == 0, f"unbalanced {sym}: {total}" # pages ops immediately
steps.decision: integrity check passed — proceed to file generation

steps.title: End-of-day bars + tape snapshotted for historical record
steps.action: In parallel with clearing, the TSDB takes its end-of-day snapshot: daily OHLCV bar for every symbol, and the raw tape is marked immutable. These are the records that will be served to charting clients for years.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- daily bar from 1-minute bars
INSERT INTO bars_1d (symbol, trade_date, open, high, low, close, volume)
SELECT symbol, '2026-04-24'::date, first_value(open) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY bucket_start), max(high), min(low), last_value(close) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY bucket_start), sum(volume)
FROM bars_1m
WHERE bucket_start >= '2026-04-24T13:30Z' AND bucket_start < '2026-04-24T20:00Z'
GROUP BY symbol;

steps.title: Generate and submit clearing file to DTCC/NSCC
steps.action: Format the nets into the clearinghouse's expected format (NSCC CNS in US) and submit via the clearinghouse's secure link. Settlement happens T+1 — i.e. positions become final next business day.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Write CNS (Continuous Net Settlement) file
with open(f"cns_2026_04_24.txt", "w") as f: for (firm, symbol), pos in sorted(nets.items): if pos["net_qty"] == 0: continue # fully offset intraday — nothing to settle f.write(f"{firm:<8}{symbol:<8}{pos['net_qty']:+012d}{pos['net_notional_minor']:+018d}\n") # Submit over secure FTP/SWIFT
upload("dtcc-sftp.dtcc.com", f"cns_2026_04_24.txt", client_cert=nscc_cert)
steps.note: The exchange's job ends at submission. The clearinghouse takes over: allocates transfers, handles fails-to-deliver, manages buy-ins. Next business day, shares and cash change hands for real.

tradeoffs.decision: Single-threaded matching per symbol vs parallel matching
tradeoffs.chosen: Single-threaded, one symbol per CPU core, pinned and isolated from the OS scheduler
tradeoffs.rationale: Price-time priority requires a single global order over events in a symbol. Any concurrent matching reintroduces reordering that violates the priority rule. We scale horizontally across symbols, not within them — a single core sustains 1M+ orders/s in practice, which is plenty per symbol.

tradeoffs.decision: Durability: synchronous disk write vs replicated log
tradeoffs.chosen: Replicated sequenced log (Aeron/custom multicast) with quorum ack, no disk on the critical path
tradeoffs.rationale: A fsync-to-disk on every order costs milliseconds, which is an eternity at exchange latency. Replicating to N+1 in-memory followers over low-latency transport gives the same durability guarantee (survives any single failure) in microseconds. The log is snapshotted to disk asynchronously for restart.

tradeoffs.decision: Strong consistency vs partition tolerance during a network split
tradeoffs.chosen: CP: if the primary loses quorum with its replicas, it stops accepting orders
tradeoffs.rationale: Two matching engines accepting orders during a partition would produce conflicting fills that can never be reconciled. Halting is expensive (market closed for that symbol for seconds) but recoverable; split brain is not.

tradeoffs.decision: Multicast market data vs per-client TCP streams
tradeoffs.chosen: UDP multicast for all subscribers on the same trading venue, TCP retransmit gap-fill server for recovery
tradeoffs.rationale: 1000 subscribers on TCP means 1000 copies of every delta out of the publisher NIC. Multicast emits once and the switch fabric fans out. Cost is UDP loss — handled by a sequence-numbered protocol with a gap-fill service for missed packets.

tradeoffs.decision: In-memory book vs persistent book per event
tradeoffs.chosen: In-memory book, end-of-day snapshot plus continuous event log
tradeoffs.rationale: The sequenced log IS the durable record. Rebuilding the book on restart means replaying the log from the last snapshot, which takes seconds even for full-day volume. Writing the book to durable storage on every event would destroy the latency budget.

interviewFollowUps.question: Opening and closing auctions with an uncrossing algorithm that maximizes executed volume
Self-trade prevention: cancel or reprice orders that would match against the same beneficiary
Iceberg orders with a hidden reserve quantity that refills the visible displayed size
Circuit breakers: auto-halt per symbol or market-wide on large adverse price moves
Regulatory reporting (MiFID II, CAT) with nanosecond-precision order lifecycle capture
Cross-datacenter disaster recovery with consistent cutover and no duplicate fills
